summary: In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays in deep anguish that the cup might pass from Him, yields to His Father’s will, and finds His disciples asleep.
key_insight: Jesus warned His disciples to watch and pray “lest you enter into temptation.” He did exactly that, and when the soldiers came He was ready. They slept, and minutes later they all ran.
story: After the supper, Jesus went out with His disciples over the Brook Kidron to a garden {Jn} on the Mount of Olives, as He was accustomed. {Lk} The place was called Gethsemane. He told the disciples, “Sit here while I go and pray over there.” {Mt} “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.” {Lk}
He took Peter, James and John with Him, and He began to be troubled and deeply distressed. {Mk} “My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death,” He told them. “Stay here and watch with Me.” {Mt}

He went a little farther, about a stone’s throw, {Lk} fell on His face, {Mt} and prayed that if it were possible, the hour might pass from Him. “Abba, Father, all things are possible for You. Take this cup away from Me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what You will.” {Mk} An angel appeared to Him from heaven, strengthening Him. Being in agony, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground. {Lk}

He came back and found them sleeping, {Mk} worn out with sorrow. {Lk} “Simon, are you sleeping?” He said to Peter. “Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” {Mk}

A second time He went away and prayed, “O My Father, if this cup cannot pass away from Me unless I drink it, Your will be done.” {Mt} Again He found them asleep, for their eyes were heavy, and they did not know what to answer Him. {Mk} So He left them and prayed a third time, saying the same words. {Mt}

Then He came the third time. “Are you still sleeping and resting? It is enough! The hour has come; behold, the Son of Man is being betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going. See, My betrayer is at hand.” {Mk}
differences: Matthew and Mark record three prayers and three returns to the sleeping disciples; Luke tells of one prayer and one return. John mentions only the garden across the Kidron.

The words of the first prayer vary: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for You” (Mark), “O My Father, if it is possible” (Matthew), “Father, if it is Your will” (Luke). Only Matthew gives the words of the second prayer.
Only Luke records the angel, the agony, the sweat like drops of blood, the distance of a stone’s throw, and that the disciples slept “from sorrow.”
Matthew and Mark say Jesus took Peter, James and John farther with Him; Luke does not mention the three. Only Mark records “Simon, are you sleeping?” and “It is enough!”

fit.question: The Gospels give the words of Jesus’ prayer in three slightly different forms. Which words did He actually pray?

points.label: A long prayer, prayed three times
points.text: Jesus prayed for about an hour (Matthew 26:40), and He went back to pray three times, “saying the same words” (Matthew 26:44). No one recorded the whole prayer; each writer gives its heart.

points.label: The same two requests
points.text: Every form has the same two parts: take this cup away, and yet let the Father’s will be done. Mark keeps the Aramaic “Abba”; Matthew and Luke put it in Greek. The variations are the kind honest witnesses give when they report what was said rather than recite it.

fit.note: The Gospels agree on what Jesus asked and how He yielded; they summarize a long prayer in their own words.
fit.short: Jesus prayed at length, three times. Each Gospel gives the heart of it: take this cup away, yet Your will be done.

scene.label: Gethsemane
scene.text: The name means an oil press. It was an olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, facing the temple across the Kidron Valley. Luke says Jesus went there “as He was accustomed,” and Judas knew the place (John 18:2).

scene.label: The cup
scene.text: In the Prophets, the cup in the LORD’s hand is His judgment on sin. Jerusalem had drunk “the cup of His fury” (Isaiah 51:17), and the nations would drink it too (Jeremiah 25:15). Jesus shrank from more than pain; He was facing that cup.

scene.label: “Abba”
scene.text: Abba is the Aramaic word a child used for “father,” warm and personal. Mark kept it untranslated. Paul says that by the Spirit believers now cry out, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6).

scene.label: David’s road
scene.text: A thousand years earlier King David, betrayed by his own counselor Ahithophel, crossed the Brook Kidron and went up the Mount of Olives weeping (2 Samuel 15:23, 30–31). Now the Son of David crossed the same valley on the night of His betrayal.

scene.label: Luke 22:43–44
scene.text: The NKJV includes these two verses, the angel and the sweat like drops of blood, and notes that some old manuscripts do not have them.

witnesses.matthew: Shows Jesus’ prayer moving from “if it is possible, let this cup pass” to “if this cup cannot pass away from Me unless I drink it, Your will be done.” Only Matthew records the second prayer and the words “watch with Me.” The King of Matthew’s Gospel goes to His throne by way of a Son’s obedience.
witnesses.mark: Keeps the raw words: Jesus was “troubled and deeply distressed,” and He prayed “Abba.” Mark shows Peter addressed by his old name, “Simon,” and the disciples with nothing to say. Peter was one of the three in the garden, and Mark likely heard this from him.
witnesses.luke: Frames the scene with one command, given at the start and again at the end: pray that you may not enter into temptation. Luke, who often shows Jesus at prayer, records the angel and the agony, and he says the disciples slept “from sorrow,” which is gentle toward them.
witnesses.john: Records only that Jesus crossed the Kidron to a garden. John had already shown Jesus troubled at the coming hour (John 12:27), and minutes later Jesus will speak of “the cup which My Father has given Me” (John 18:11), words that assume the prayer the others record.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is fully human, overwhelmed with sorrow and shrinking from the cup, and He is the obedient Son, who chooses His Father’s will with His eyes open to what it will cost.
seeing.living: Jesus did not hide His distress; He told His friends His soul was sorrowful to death and told His Father exactly what He wanted. Bring God your honest request, and then pray the harder words, “not what I will, but what You will.” When you fail to watch, remember the One who did not fail.
seeing.ponder: Is there a cup you are asking God to take away? Can you pray honestly for it to pass and still say, “Your will be done”?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus asked for the cup to pass, then rose to drink it: the Son chose the Father’s will.
outline: A Savior who rises to meet the hour (41–42)
preaching.watch_for: On Tuesday, on this same Mount of Olives, Jesus ended His teaching with a warning that the master might come “at the crowing of the rooster,” and “lest, coming suddenly, he find you sleeping” (Mark 13:35–36). In Gethsemane He comes back three times and finds them sleeping.
